script: Don't want me to do the work myself? Ok, then run and do it yourself.. I worked at a buffet restaurant, and every shift we were split up into one‑liners: cashier, runner, cleaner, dishwasher. I was the runner because I could sprint the 50‑foot run from the kitchen to the counter faster than anyone. The rule was simple: grab the food and be back in three minutes or the manager would ping the kitchen and we'd all get the heat. We had a counter between the kitchen and the corridor that the cart slid on. Usually you ask, they drop the plates on the counter in a minute, you load the cart, and boom, back to the dining area. But if the kitchen was short‑staffed and we needed sauces, green onions, or a jar of jam, we'd just waltz in and grab what we needed. It wasn't a rule, more like a tacit understanding that had worked for years. So one shift we needed a handful of sauces and a bag of green onions. I'd asked for them, waited a minute, and shouted, "Coming in! Grabbing green onions!" and strutted into the kitchen. (I was about to grab the green onions when the chef screamed.) He stormed toward me, yelling that I was in the wrong zone and that it wasn't my job. "You're not supposed to touch anything," he hissed. I asked why because we'd always done it. He said it was his job, and that I should only ask and wait. So the next time I needed something, I marched in, the chef was prepping something else, and I started screaming the list: "Sauce One, Sauce Two, Green Onions, Honey, This, That, This Also, Something Else." I knew the spots, so I could have grabbed it while I was yelling. The chef didn't say anything for a few seconds, so I blew the list out again. On the third time, while he was grabbing a sauce and putting it on the counter, he said, "It's just me here, stop screaming and just put the paper there and wait." I responded, "I've got to be back in three minutes or the manager will call and I'll have to explain why you're taking forever." He said, "Ok, just go in there and grab it." I reminded him he'd told me the other day I wasn't supposed to touch anything. He changed his mind, said, "Forget it, just do it." I told him I'd have to call the leader to confirm I was allowed. He ran around the kitchen, gathered everything I needed, and never complained about us being inside. When he finally handed over the sauce, I realized the audacity of the kitchen hierarchy. The whole thing was a reminder that even in a place that runs on routine, the power dynamics can still surprise you.
